t.7.32.1: Not far from that place on the bank of the Narmadā where Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, was making his offering of flowers,
t.7.32.2: Arjuna, the best of victors, the mighty lord of Māhiṣmatī, is sporting with his women, having entered the waters of the Narmadā.
t.7.32.3: Then King Arjuna, standing in the midst of those women, shone splendidly, like a bull elephant standing in the midst of a thousand female elephants.
t.7.32.4: Wishing to know the supreme strength of his thousand arms, Arjuna then checked the rushing current of the Narmadā with his arms.
t.7.32.5: That clear water, on reaching the dam formed by Kārtavīrya's arms, rushes back against the current, carrying away its banks.
t.7.32.6: That rushing current of the Narmadā's waters, bearing fish, crocodiles and makaras along with a spread of flowers and kuśa grass, shone as if it were the rainy season.
t.7.32.7: That rush of water, as though sent forth by Kārtavīrya himself, swept away the entire offering of flowers made by Rāvaṇa.
t.7.32.8: Then Rāvaṇa, abandoning his half-finished observance, gazed upon the lovely Narmadā, now flowing against her course, as one would look upon a beloved woman who has turned contrary.
t.7.32.9: But having seen from the west that swelling rush of water, resembling the outpouring of the ocean, and having entered the eastern quarter…
t.7.32.10: Then Rāvaṇa beheld the river, its birds untroubled, abiding in its own supreme natural state, resembling a woman free of all agitation.
t.7.32.11: Then Daśānana, with a finger of his right hand and with a sound, directed Śuka and Sāraṇa to search out the source of the surging flood.
t.7.32.12: But those two brothers, the heroes Śuka and Sāraṇa, commanded by Rāvaṇa, moving through the expanse of the sky, set out with their faces turned toward the west.
t.7.32.13: Having gone only half a yojana, those two night-rovers saw a man sporting in the water together with women.
t.7.32.14: Him, resembling a great sāla tree, his hair tossed about by the water, the corners of his eyes reddened with intoxication, and his splendour like the form of Madana himself.
t.7.32.15: They saw the crusher of foes damming the river with his thousand arms, like a mountain holding back the earth with its thousand feet.
t.7.32.16: He was surrounded by a thousand young and excellent women, like a bull elephant surrounded by a thousand female elephants in rut.
t.7.32.17: Having seen that most wondrous one, the two Rākṣasas Śuka and Sāraṇa turned back, approached Rāvaṇa, and then spoke to him.
t.7.32.18: O lord of the Rākṣasas, someone who looks like a mighty sāla tree has dammed the Narmadā as though with an embankment and is making the women sport there.
t.7.32.19: Its waters dammed by that thousand of arms, the river again and again sent forth surges like the upheavals of the ocean.
t.7.32.20: Hearing Śuka and Sāraṇa speaking thus, Rāvaṇa exclaimed, "Arjuna!" and rose up, eager for battle.
t.7.32.21: As that lord of the Rākṣasas set out to face Arjuna, the clouds at once raised a roar and sent it forth together with a shower of blood.
t.7.32.22: Then the lord of the Rākṣasas, surrounded by Mahodara, Mahāpārśva, Dhūmrākṣa, Śuka and Sāraṇa, went to the place where that Arjuna was.
t.7.32.23: Then, after no very long time, that mighty Rākṣasa, dark as collyrium, came to that fearsome pool of the Narmadā.
t.7.32.24: There the king of the Rākṣasas then beheld Arjuna, lord of men, surrounded by women like an elephant surrounded by she-elephants in heat.
t.7.32.25: That lord of the Rākṣasas, his eyes red with rage and swollen with pride in his strength, spoke thus in a deep voice to the ministers of Arjuna.
t.7.32.26: O ministers, quickly announce to the Haihaya king that one called Rāvaṇa by name has arrived here for battle.
t.7.32.27: Having heard Rāvaṇa's words, the ministers of Arjuna then rose up, weapons in hand, and spoke these words to Rāvaṇa.
t.7.32.28: Well done, O Rāvaṇa, well done! You have recognized the right time for battle, you who wish to fight our king while he is intoxicated and surrounded by women, like a tiger attacking an elephant in rut standing amid his she-elephants.
t.7.32.29: Be patient today, O Daśagrīva, and spend the night here; but if you have a desire for battle, then tomorrow, dear one, you may meet Arjuna in combat.
t.7.32.30: Or if you are in haste, overcome by thirst for battle, then only after slaying us will you come to battle with Arjuna.
t.7.32.31: Then the ministers of the king were slain in battle by Rāvaṇa's ministers, and they were devoured by those hungry ones.
t.7.32.32: Then on the bank of the Narmadā there arose a tumultuous uproar from the followers of Arjuna and the ministers of Rāvaṇa.
t.7.32.33: Rushing upon them from all sides, they harassed Rāvaṇa and his followers with arrows, lances and thunderbolt-like spears, together with grappling hooks.
t.7.32.34: The onslaught of the warriors of the lord of the Haihayas was exceedingly terrible, and its roar was like that of the ocean teeming with crocodiles, fish and makaras.
t.7.32.35: But those ministers of Rāvaṇa, Prahasta, Śuka and Sāraṇa, enraged and blazing with the splendour of fire, burn up the army of Kārtavīrya.
t.7.32.36: That deed of Rāvaṇa and his ministers was reported to Arjuna, who was sporting at play, by the men who guarded the gates.
t.7.32.37: Having told the women, "Do not be afraid," Arjuna then rose up out of that water, like Añjana emerging from the waters of the Gaṅgā.
t.7.32.39: He, wearing armlets of the finest gold, swiftly seized his mace and charged at the Rākṣasas, as the sun rushes upon the darkness.
t.7.32.38: Then Arjuna, that fire, his eyes inflamed with rage, blazed up exceedingly terrible, like the fire at the end of a yuga.
t.7.32.41: Blocking his path as the Vindhya mountain once blocked the path of the sun, Prahasta, armed with a club, stood there immovable like the Vindhya.
t.7.32.40: Raising high his great mace, which was wielded with a sweeping swing of the arms, and taking on the speed of Garuḍa, that Arjuna swooped down to attack.
t.7.32.42: Then Prahasta, frenzied with pride and enraged, hurled at him a terrible iron-bound club and roared like a rain-cloud.
t.7.32.43: At the tip of that club hurled from Prahasta's hand, a fire arose like a chaplet of red aśoka blossoms, as if it were burning everything up.
t.7.32.44: Then Kārtavīrya Arjuna, mace in hand and mighty as an elephant, skillfully evaded the club as it came rushing at him.
t.7.32.45: Then the lord of the Haihayas rushed at Prahasta, whirling a heavy mace that rose five hundred arm-lengths high.
t.7.32.46: Struck then by him with the mace with great force, Prahasta fell down, like a standing mountain struck by the thunderbolt of the wielder of the thunderbolt.
t.7.32.47: Seeing Prahasta fallen, Mārīca, Śuka and Sāraṇa, together with Mahodara and Dhūmrākṣa, withdrew from the field of battle.
t.7.32.48: When the ministers had fled and Prahasta had been struck down, Rāvaṇa swiftly rushed at Arjuna, the best of kings.
t.7.32.49: There began that dreadful, hair-raising battle between the thousand-armed one and the twenty-armed one, between the king and the rākṣasa.
t.7.32.50: The two were like two oceans churned into turmoil, like two mountains whose roots were shaken, like two suns full of radiance, like two fires burning everything around them.
t.7.32.51: They were like two elephants swollen with might, like two bulls contending for a cow, roaring like two thunderclouds, and fierce in strength like two lions.
t.7.32.52: Enraged like Rudra and Kāla, the two of them, the Rākṣasa and Arjuna, struck each other fiercely with their maces.
t.7.32.53: Just as the mountains once endured the terrible blows of the thunderbolt, so did those two, the man and the Rākṣasa, endure the blows of the maces.
t.7.32.54: Just as an echo arises from the crashing of thunderbolts, so all the directions echoed with the blows of the maces struck by those two.
t.7.32.55: But that mace of Arjuna, as it was brought down upon the chest of his foe, made the sky gleam like gold, as a flash of lightning does.
t.7.32.56: In the same way, the mace brought down again and again by Rāvaṇa upon Arjuna's chest shone like a meteor falling upon a great mountain.
t.7.32.57: Neither Arjuna nor the lord of the hosts of Rākṣasas grew weary; the battle between the two was evenly matched, as was that of Bali and Indra of old.
t.7.32.58: Like two great bulls goring each other with their horns, or like two elephants striking with the tips of their tusks, the foremost of men and the foremost of rākṣasas struck at one another.
t.7.32.59: Then, in that great battle, the enraged Arjuna, with all his strength, hurled that mace between the breasts of Rāvaṇa.
t.7.32.60: Striking Rāvaṇa's chest, which was shielded by the granting of a boon, that mace broke in two like a feeble army and fell to the ground.
t.7.32.61: But Rāvaṇa, struck by the blow of the mace hurled by Arjuna, fell back the length of a bow and sank down, groaning.
t.7.32.62: Then Arjuna, seeing Daśagrīva thus staggering, suddenly seized him, as Garutmant seizes a serpent.
t.7.32.63: That mighty king, seizing the Ten-faced one by force with his thousand arms, bound him, just as Nārāyaṇa bound Bali.
t.7.32.64: As Daśagrīva was being bound, the Siddhas, Cāraṇas and deities, crying "Well done!", showered flowers upon Arjuna's head.
t.7.32.65: Like a tiger seizing a deer, like the king of lions seizing an elephant, the Haihaya king, having seized him, roared again and again in delight like a rain-cloud.
t.7.32.66: But Prahasta, having recovered himself and seeing the ten-faced Rāvaṇa bound, rushed in fury at the king together with those rākṣasas.
t.7.32.67: The onrush of those night-rangers as they swooped down appeared wondrous, like the surging of the oceans when the end of the hot season has set in.
t.7.32.68: Crying again and again, "Let him go, let him go!" and "Stop, stop!", they then hurled pestles and spears at Arjuna.
t.7.32.69: Then Arjuna, the slayer of foes, unperturbed, swiftly seized those weapons of the enemies of the gods before they had even reached him.
t.7.32.70: Then, with those very irresistible and excellent weapons, he pierced the Rākṣasas and put them to flight, as the wind scatters the clouds.
t.7.32.71: Then Kārtavīryārjuna, having terrified the Rākṣasas and seized Rāvaṇa, entered his city, surrounded by his friends.
t.7.32.72: Then Arjuna, resembling Puruhūta, showered with heaps of flowers and unbroken grains by the twice-born together with the citizens, entered that city, like the thousand-eyed one after seizing Bali.
